newsitem.title: UK: African refugee crisis worsened in 1996 - Amnesty.
newsitem.headline: African refugee crisis worsened in 1996 - Amnesty.

text.p: Amnesty International said on Wednesday Africa's refugee crisis worsened last year, following mass killings and political unrest which forced hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes.

The London-based human rights group said in its annual report that armed opposition groups tortured and killed people in a dozen African countries including Burundi, Angola, Chad, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Zaire.
"In Africa alone there are five million refugees -- one third of the world's total -- and at least 16 million internally displaced people," Amnesty said.
"These countries are among the world's poorest, and yet they have been left to bear the enormous logistic, economic and environmental strains that result from mass flows of refugees."

In Burundi, tens of thousands of unarmed civilians were killed by the security forces, by Tutsi groups acting in collusion with the government forces and by armed Hutu opposition groups, Amnesty said.

Children and infants were among the victims in Rwanda when opposition groups slaughtered unarmed civilians. Amnesty said by the end of last year nearly 100,000 people were detained, many without charge, in overcrowded conditions which led to many deaths.
When fighting broke out in eastern Zaire towards the end of last year more than one million refugees from Rwanda and Burundi faced starvation.
Amnesty said thousands of unarmed refugees and Zairians were reportedly killed by the Alliance of the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL).
It urged world governments to halt the supply of weapons in the region and called for an international presence in Burundi, Rwanda and eastern Zaire to protect civilians.
"Decades of atrocities have set populations against each other in Africa's Great Lakes region.

"But the many disparate groups from Rwanda, Zaire and Burundi have one thing in common: they are in grave danger of continued human rights abuses and they are not getting from states and intergovernmental organisations the full protection which is due to refugees under regional and international treaties," Amnesty said.
Human rights abuses were also committed in Liberia and Sierra Leone where defenceless people were tortured and killed, the group added.

In Nigeria, prisoners of conscience were still being detained despite an international uproar following the execution of writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other activists from the Movement for the Survival of Ogoni Peoples.
